task: Deciding tensor rank as a satisfiability question: is there a decomposition of T into k rank-one terms?
source: Produced by `reproduce/measure.py`, which asks every question below of both instruments: `decide-rank-by-sat <fixture> --target k --break-symmetry --plain-cnf` for the solver columns, and `decide-rank <fixture> --target k [--node-limit N]` for the exhaustive ones, which answer the same question by enumerating subspaces. Each row carries the invocation that produced it, node limit and all, and the driver reads that line back rather than rebuilding it, and the provenance block at the end names the commit, the compiler, the Givaro version, the solvers on PATH and the defaults in force.
covered: `measure.py --check` re-derives `found_at`, `ruled_out_at` and `exhaustive_nodes`, and stops the run rather than reporting drift if a verdict has flipped. It carries `field`, `known_rank`, the notes and the `*_under_cryptominisat` second opinions untouched, because those are a literature fact, prose and another solver's answer rather than measurements this driver makes. It re-derives no timing, for the reason MEASURING.md gives. Every count here is reproducible, but one is not re-derived by default: the GF(16) exhaustive node count is 6.6 minutes of one core, so `--check` carries it and `--check --slow` asks it, and a SKIPPED line names that figure and its price on every run.
why: Hastad proved in 1990 that tensor rank is NP-complete over every finite field. NP-completeness cuts both ways: a decomposition is a certificate, so the question can be handed to a solver rather than enumerated.
machine: Single core of a 12th Gen Intel i5-12450H at 2.2 GHz, 2026-08-16. Every timing is the fastest of three runs on an otherwise quiet machine, because the spread between runs is larger than several of the values.
timings: Every `*_seconds` field is the 2026-08-16 run described under `machine`, and no `--check` reads one. They are rewritten only by a full `measure.py` run on a quiet machine, under the protocol in MEASURING.md; the counts beside them are re-derived on every push.
solver: kissat 4.0.4, and every `*_seconds` field is kissat unless its name says otherwise. Some of these were previously cryptominisat timings under a heading that said kissat, which is why the solver is now named per column: `*_under_cryptominisat` fields are the second opinion and the evidence for preferring kissat, kept rather than deleted because without them the preference has nothing behind it.
solver_choice: Native XOR clauses are worth nothing on these instances, 1.559 s against 1.563 s on the same question. Raw strength is worth 134x on the dearest find here, GF(16) at 9 products: 0.270 s against 36.19 s. See `choices/`.
methods: GF(2): Boolean variables per coordinate, Tseitin conjunctions in two stages, one parity constraint per tensor entry.
GF(p) one-hot: p Booleans per unknown with exactly one true, and the field's multiplication and addition tables written out as implications.
GF(p) field theory: the equations handed to cvc5's decision procedure for prime fields, with no encoding of the field at all.
caveat: A no is a lower bound only if the solver finished. Timeouts and memory kills are a third verdict and are never folded into no. A yes is checked: the model is turned back into rank-one matrices and recombined against the tensor.

fixtures.name: gf8_multiplication
fixtures.note: The 4.13 s recorded here for ruling out 5 could not be reproduced by anything tried: 0.0378 s with the term ordering, 0.534 s without it, 0.0357 s under cryptominisat. It is replaced rather than explained, and said so here so the next reader does not inherit the same puzzle. `search/` was the file that was right: its gf8 floor of 0.085 s is the sum of these two questions.

fixtures.name: matmul_2x2x3
fixtures.exhaustive_note: The tree search opens no node here any more, and that is a real change rather than a lost measurement. `rank_lower_bound` is the maximum over the flattening rank and `[yang2025]`'s two rank sums, and it puts this tensor at 9, so `decide-rank --target 8` refutes the target by Gaussian elimination and returns before the search opens a node. There is therefore no search time to report. The 446 923 nodes and 53.1 s this row carried before were what the same command produced when the flattening rank was the only bound it had; no invocation of the shipped binary produces them now.

fixtures.name: gf16_multiplication
fixtures.exhaustive_note: The node count is reproducible now and the flag behind it is in `exhaustive_command` above: the missing `--node-limit` was 200 000 000, and the recorded line gives 105 600 301 nodes and exit 1, deterministically, matching this row exactly. `reproduce/measure.py` reads that field back rather than rebuilding the line, so the flag is passed again; what it no longer does by default is spend the 6.6 minutes of one core the search costs, which is longer than every other question in this file together, so the default run carries this count and `--slow` re-derives it. The SKIPPED line names the price. **The 2328 s beside the count is older than the count's own instrument** and is left as measured rather than replaced: it was taken before the GF(2) bit-packed leaf existed (`exhaustive_search/gf2_leaf.h`), and at the general-leaf rate that file records, 200 000 nodes in 4.47 s, this count projects to 2360 s, which is the recorded value inside the 13% thermal band. The shipped binary does the same search about six times faster, but no replacement timing is published here: the runs that showed it were taken on a machine with a browser on it, which MEASURING.md does not accept.

fixtures.name: f2_5x5
fixtures.known_rank_note: 13, established in this repository on both sides: 12 products ruled out exhaustively, and 13 exhibited by lower-the-bound in 80 nodes. The heuristic reaches only 14.
fixtures.note: Unresolved here. No answer in 700 s of one core, and no proof written. The exhaustive search has not run k=12 either; its 7 h figure is an extrapolation from k=11, not a measurement.

prime_field_backends.note: Ground truth from the exhaustive search. Every verdict both backends produced agrees, which is what the second backend is for.

symmetry_breaking.note: Ordering the terms is sound, since permuting a decomposition gives another decomposition, and it was checked against all six fixtures of known rank before being trusted. Off by default because an over-strong constraint would turn a satisfiable instance into UNSAT, which is a wrong lower bound.
symmetry_breaking.question: matmul_2x2x2, rule out 6
symmetry_breaking.worth: 79x, and both ends of that are finite measurements under the shipped solver.
symmetry_breaking.cryptominisat_note: No answer in 120 s without the ordering, 1.57 s with it, which is where the earlier `at least 76x` came from. The pair is kept because it is a lower bound on the same effect from the other solver, and labelled because the file used to present it as kissat's.

provenance.protocol: one core, fastest of three, quiet machine. See MEASURING.md.

counts_provenance.covers: The counts in this file and the invocations that produced them, and nothing else. Every `seconds` field here is older than this block and was not touched: a count is exact arithmetic and comes out the same on any machine, a timing does not, so `--counts` refreshes the first and leaves the second exactly as measured. What produced the timings is the `provenance` block.
counts_provenance.protocol: counts only: exact arithmetic, one run each, the machine irrelevant.
